title: Orchestration Adaptors for Typed Output and Tool Reconciliation (PRD Draft)
content:
Purpose
This PRD draft proposes a lightweight orchestration adaptor layer for the Hosted API that:
- makes structured/typed output first-class in streaming responses,
- provides an explicit reconciliation protocol for tool calls (tool invocation, tool result reconciliation, retries), and
- exposes ergonomic client-side SDK primitives (thin adapters) that enable graceful degradation and predictable latency budgets for low-bandwidth or mobile clients.

Why this work now
We continue to see customers building complex tool-driven experiences (search+api calls, DB lookups, ticket creation) that require precise, machine-readable output and deterministic handling of partial/failed tool invocations. Current hosted streaming surfaces are powerful but leave a lot of client implementation burden: parsing ad-hoc tokens, detecting tool boundaries, reconciling out-of-order tool responses, and implementing retry/backoff strategies. That leads to bugs, poor UX, and duplicate engineering across customers.

Goals (measurable)
- Developer ergonomics: reduce average customer integration time for tool-driven flows by 40% (tracked via support tickets and onboarding tests).
- Correctness: achieve a 90% reduction in customer-reported parsing/reconciliation bugs for tool flows in pilot cohort.
- Latency preservation: add typed-output and reconciliation without increasing median token-to-tool-latency by more than 8%.
- Cost: additional platform CPU overhead should be <5% for typical streaming workloads.

Non-goals
- This PRD does not propose a replacement of the full streaming framing (we keep the existing incremental-token stream for backward compatibility).
- It does not mandate a single schema language (we support JSON Schema-first and a simple typed DSL).

User personas and example flows
1) Mobile product team wanting robust tool calls: a mobile app issues a chat request that may require calling a payment API and a shipping API. The app needs deterministic acknowledgement that a tool was invoked, a way to surface partial progress to users, and a fallback if the payment API times out.
2) Platform integrator embedding Redwood in an automation pipeline: orchestrates multiple stepwise tool calls, wants machine-readable deltas for idempotency and replay.
3) Developer prototyping a compose UI: needs typed output so UI components can render results without custom parsing.

High-level approach
Introduce a small adaptor layer between the serving runtime and the streaming output that:
- Emits typed frames in the streaming response (distinct from free-form text tokens) with explicit lifecycle states (open, emitted, confirmed, reconciled, failed).
- Defines a tool-operation reconciliation protocol: each tool call gets an operation id (op_id), a declared intent (tool_name + typed args), and a status stream that transitions through states with optional result payloads.
- Exposes lightweight client SDK adaptors that interpret typed frames, provide callback hooks for tool lifecycle events, and surface helper utilities for local retry/backoff and UI-friendly progress.

API and wire-level sketch (stream framing)
We propose adding an opt-in typed-frame envelope yielded as part of the streaming response. The envelope is separate from token deltas and coexists with existing streaming to preserve backwards compatibility. Clients may request typed frames via a query param or header: 
- header: X-RW-Typed-Frames: true
- param: typed_frames=true

Example envelope sequence (newline-delimited JSON for streaming RTT):
{
  "frame_type": "text_delta",
  "delta": "Sure, I can do that. First I'll call the payment tool..."
}
{
  "frame_type": "tool_op",
  "op_id": "op_7b2f",
  "tool": "payment.charge",
  "args": {"amount": 34.5, "currency": "USD"},
  "state": "issued"
}
{
  "frame_type": "progress",
  "op_id": "op_7b2f",
  "state": "in_flight",
  "hint": "waiting-on-3rd-party"
}
{
  "frame_type": "tool_result",
  "op_id": "op_7b2f",
  "state": "succeeded",
  "result": {"charge_id": "ch_01AZ", "status": "completed"}
}
{
  "frame_type": "text_delta",
  "delta": "Payment succeeded — booking confirmed!"
}

Contract notes: op_id must be globally unique per request, state transitions must follow a deterministic set (issued -> in_flight -> succeeded|failed|timed_out|reconciled). Tool result payloads should be small; large binary blobs are returned as signed URLs.

Reconciliation rules and retries
- Deterministic idempotency: op_id + request_id forms an idempotency key for tool providers. Hosted API will surface a recommended idempotency header to the customer’s tool integration.
- Soft-fallback policy: if a tool call fails or times out, the runtime will emit a tool_result with state=failed and a normalized failure_code (e.g., TIMEOUT, AUTH_ERROR, PERMISSION). Client SDK adaptors provide helpers to optionally: retry with backoff (configurable by developer), prompt the model to synthesize an alternate plan, or escalate to human review.
- Reconciliation window: by default 60s after a tool_result is emitted, the reconcile endpoint can be called to reconcile out-of-band confirmations from the integrator.

SDK ergonomics (thin adaptors)
We propose a family of small client-side helpers shipped in each language SDK:
- TypedStreamReader: takes the raw streaming socket and yields a mixed sequence of TokenDelta or TypedFrame objects.
- ToolLifecycleListener: pub/sub callbacks for onIssued(op), onProgress(op, hint), onResult(op, result), onFailed(op, code).
- LocalReplayStore: optional simple local LRU store that keeps recent op_id -> state to support offline reconcilation and idempotent retries.
- GracefulDegradationPolicy: declarative rules (maxLatencyMillis, fallbackMode: synthesize_text | skip_tool | queue_for_retry) that the SDK enforces when network or tool latencies exceed thresholds.

Developer experience examples
1) Minimal: mobile client opts into typed frames and binds ToolLifecycleListener to show spinners for ops; fallbackMode= synthesize_text. No server changes needed.
2) Advanced: server-side integrator implements op idempotency and uses reconcile endpoint to confirm charges asynchronously. Client SDK sets LocalReplayStore={size:100, ttl:300s}.

Server-side changes (summary)
- Small framing layer in serving runtime to emit typed frames.
- Tool orchestration coordinator (lightweight): issues op_ids, routes op events, enforces idemp rules and emits normalized failure codes.
- Optional reconcile endpoint that accepts confirm/reject payloads for previously emitted op_ids.

Observability and telemetry
- Emit per-op telemetry: op_latency_ms, op_outcome, tool_name, failure_code.
- Expose new console views: tool-operation timelines, per-customer reconciliation rates, and top failure modes.
- Provide sample Grafana/Traces queries for common debugging flows.

Security and privacy considerations
- Tool args and results may contain PII. Default behavior: redact recognized PII in telemetry and logs; provide a knob in Dedicated/Private to forward full payloads to customer-managed logging only if they opt-in.
- Signed URL gating for large payloads; ephemeral tokens; HMAC for reconcile callbacks recommended.

Migration and compatibility
- Backwards compatible: if client does not request typed frames, tokens-only streaming continues.
- Tiered rollout: alpha for early partners (Dedicated + Hosted pilot), beta with console toggles, GA after 8–12 weeks of pilot telemetry.

Success metrics and rollout plan
- Pilot cohort (3 customers): measure decrease in integration bugs and average integrate time; iterate SDK ergonomics.
- Beta (20 customers): track op success rates, reconcile latency, 95th percentile token-to-tool latency.
- GA threshold: <8% latency increase, <5% added CPU, reduction in tool-related support tickets by 60% among pilot customers.

Open questions / tradeoffs
- Should we mandate a single schema language? (Tradeoff: fragmentation vs locking customers into schema.) Proposed compromise: default JSON Schema + opt-in typed DSL for compactness.
- Reconcile window length: 60s vs longer windows for offline tools. We allow configurability per tool integration but recommend 60s for real-time flows.
- Where should op state live for Private deployments? Default: in customer-controlled storage or ephemeral RW-managed cache with export hooks.

Next steps (short term)
- Build a prototype streaming adaptor that emits typed frames in the runtime (SRE/Serving pair, 2-week spike).
- Implement JS & Kotlin client adaptors with ToolLifecycleListener + example app (mobile demo).
- Run a small pilot with 2 integrators that have complex tool flows.

Appendix: Short sample SDK snippet (pseudo-code)
// subscribe to typed stream
const reader = new TypedStreamReader(ws);
reader.on('token', t => ui.append(t));
reader.on('tool', op => {
  lifecycle.onIssued(op);
});
reader.on('tool_progress', ({op_id, hint}) => {
  lifecycle.onProgress(op_id, hint);
});
reader.on('tool_result', ({op_id, result}) => {
  lifecycle.onResult(op_id, result);
});
reader.on('tool_failed', ({op_id, code}) => {
  lifecycle.onFailed(op_id, code);
});

Notes to reviewers
- This is intentionally prescriptive on framing and SDK surfaces but lightweight on schema enforcement. We want the runtime guarantees (op lifecycle, unique op_id, normalized failures) more than strict typing at launch.
- Looking for feedback on: reconcile semantics, default fallbackMode choices, and whether the SDK should include auto-retry out-of-the-box or just helpers.

Done / draft status
- Draft ready for product and serving review. Expect iterations after prototype telemetry and pilot feedback.
